en: Preface to the Direct Commentary on the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*:

The establishment of the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) of the reason penetrates to the fundamental cause of all phenomena (*dharma*). The determination of the five types of sound enters into the correct principle of all phenomena.

Thus, the three members [of the syllogism] are free from fault. The thesis (*pakṣa*) relies upon the "ability" and the "cause" to initiate the reason; when many principles are fully established, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is employed as a distinction.

They arise together to produce their fruit. If one can establish that both [the thesis and the refutation] are true, and the refuter is equally false, then even the eloquence of Zeng Shen and Huiyi could not expose its error, nor could the compositions of Lu Ji and Luo Binwang embellish its faults. For this reason, it reviles the Māras, the heterodox, and the iron-clad [heretics].
By this, they were brought to submission; by this, the Golden Wheel was guided for gods and men, and by this, they were relied upon and honored.

That which is called "the arising of speech that leads to wisdom" clearly reveals the correct and crushes the heterodox; self-awakening and awakening others do not exceed this. Therefore, within the city of Kanyākubja, [he established his position].
On the eighteenth day, he established the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*; the many sages of the various states did not dare to offer dissenting arguments.

Is this not indeed the power of the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) to realize the Truth? Tracing the origins of this treatise, it was first translated by Master Xuanzang and subsequently expounded by [Master] Yongming;

however, over time, it gradually became rare to hear of and eventually seemed to have nearly perished. Great Master Gao Yuan [Yuanxiao] distantly continued its remaining radiance, vowing to revive its essential tenets. Alas for...
The meaning and intent [of this work] are profound and subtle; when beginners encounter the text, it is difficult to understand.

Therefore, I have used straightforward language to clear the paths, so that all who read it may see the whole ox before their eyes [i.e., grasp the subject matter with complete clarity]. I have long admired these writings and rejoice at having encountered this Dharma assembly.
Though I am ashamed of my own lack of familiarity, I have acted as the master’s herald. I hope that my fellow practitioners will not let this cause perish.
Written on the second day before the Dragon Boat Festival in the year of Renzi during the Wanli era, by the junior scholar Da-shan of Wulin,
while residing among the mountains of Nanping,
in homage, as a direct commentary on the *Nyāyapraveśa*.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Śaṃkarasvāmin;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang;
annotated by the Śramaṇa Mingyu of Western Shu.
△ Now, this treatise shall be explained. The structural outline is divided into four parts: 1. Explanation of the title; 2. Explanation of the author; 3.
Explanation of the translator; 4. Explanation of the main text of the treatise. First, the title is explained.

"Cause" refers to the inferential cognition (*anumāna*) that evaluates all phenomena. "Illumination" refers to the correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) that illuminates all phenomena. Without correct wisdom, there is no means to illuminate the fundamental causes of all phenomena;
without inferential cognition, there is no means to evaluate the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.

Therefore, by relying on inferential cognition and correct wisdom, one can enter into the true principle of all phenomena. Thus, the Master of the Treatise [Vasubandhu] establishes [the existence of the past and future] through what is universally acknowledged (*prasiddha*).
The property to be proven (*sādhya*) is established as the thesis (*pakṣa*); that which is a property of the entire subject (*pakṣadharma*) is the reason (*hetu*);

and that which reveals the presence of the reason in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Is this not the *Nyāyapraveśa*? For "reason" (*hetu*) is the meaning of inference (*anumāna*), and it consists of three members.

Taking the three-membered syllogism as its cause, it is called *hetu* (reasoning); taking the arising of knowledge and comprehension as its fruit, it is called *vidyā* (science); taking the progression toward and attainment of the fundamental [truth] as its entry, it is called *praveśa* (entry);

taking the exclusion of partiality and error as its correctness, it is called *samyak* (correct); and taking the self-characteristics of all phenomena as its principle, it is called *naya* (principle). The discourse between proponent and opponent is called *vāda* (debate).
Therefore, it is titled the *Nyāyamukha-praveśa-śāstra* (The Treatise on Entering the Correct Principle through Reasoning). This is indeed the secret key for investigating the meaning [of reality].

The key, the balance, and the scale; the pivot of wondrous transformation at the boundary of wisdom. It elucidates the ultimate aim of investigation and measurement, and sets forth the model for refuting heterodoxy.
If one enters the correct principle of a single phenomenon through the *hetuvidyā* (science of reasons), one enters the correct principle of all phenomena through the *hetuvidyā*.
Once the correct principle is attained, correct wisdom becomes manifest. Thus, one is able to penetrate and exhaustively master all things.

The source of the Dharma is such that all things are without obstruction; how could it be easily described? It is only a matter of fearing that one’s realization of the Truth is not intimate and that one’s formal logical arguments (*pramāṇa*) are not authentic.
Some may claim that this scripture is unsuitable for this region, but I, being ignorant, am unable to know [the truth of such claims].
△ The first section, the explanation of the title, is concluded. Below, the second section explains the author of the treatise.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarapati.

"Śaṅkara" is the Sanskrit term; this means "Heavenly Lord" (天) in the language of Tang (Chinese). The translator retained the Sanskrit while adding the Chinese for the name, hence it is called "Heavenly Lord.
Regarding "Bodhisattva," this is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit; if expressed in full, it should be "Bodhi-sattva."

*Bodhisattva*: *Bodhi* means "awakening" (*jue*), and *sattva* means "sentient being" (*qing*). Because the author of the treatise has already awakened himself and further awakens sentient beings, he is called a *bodhisattva*.
Here, for the sake of brevity, he is simply named a "Bodhisattva. Regarding the term "composed" (*zao*):

although the Master of Meaning (the Buddha) was the first to awaken, [this work] is nonetheless produced from his own personal composition; therefore, it is said to be "composed. 2. Explanation of the Title.
The master of the treatise has concluded. Below follows the explanation of the three translators.
The Tripitaka Master Xuanzang translated the *Tripitaka*.
"Tripitaka" refers to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras. The Sūtras penetrate the principles; the Vinaya disciplines the precepts; and the Śāstras adjudicate right from wrong.
In distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox, he was equally proficient as a Dharma Master; therefore, he was titled by the name "Tripitaka.
Since he was proficient in the Tripitaka and served as a teacher to others, he was further designated by the title "Dharma Master. △ Third, the explanation of the Translator is concluded.

Below follows the fourth section, the explanation of the Treatise, which is divided into three parts: first, the general heading; second, the comprehensive explanation; third, the concluding clarification. First, the general heading:

The means of proof (*sādhana*) and the means of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), along with their fallacies (*tadābhāsa*), serve solely for the instruction of others; direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), along with their fallacies, serve solely for one's own understanding.
This verse constitutes the fundamental outline of this treatise, revealing the general summary of its eight sections and two benefits, intended for those who would study it.

This refers to knowing the essential points. One who can establish [a thesis] ensures that the three members of the syllogism are free from error. One who can refute [an opponent] correctly exposes their fallacies.

That which resembles a valid establishment is accompanied by thirty-three types of faults. That which resembles a valid refutation consists of erroneous censures such as the "uncertain" (*anaikāntika*) and the "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is defined as being free from all conceptualization associated with names and expressions. Inference (*anumāna*) is defined as relying upon...
Observing the meaning through various characteristics: that which resembles direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) functions erroneously regarding the object;
that which resembles inference (*anumāna*) cannot provide correct understanding. As for "merely awakening others," the preceding four gates all serve to demonstrate the meaning of benefiting others.

Therefore, it is said that [the first four gates] "awaken others. As for "awakening oneself alone," this refers to the latter four gates, as they all pertain to the realm of self-realization and self-understanding;
hence, it is called "awakening oneself. Thus, the two benefits of the eight gates collectively encompass the essential purport of this entire treatise.

Thus, the essential meanings of all treatises are comprehensively summarized and concluded as the subject matter expounded in this verse; it encompasses the core significance of all such works. △ The first section, the general introduction, is completed.

Below, the second section, the comprehensive explanation, is divided into eight parts: 1. The Gate of the Prover (*sādhana*); 2. The Gate of the Fallacious Prover (*sādhanābhāsa*); 3. The Gate of Direct Perception (*pratyakṣa*); 4. [The Gate of Inference]... (and so forth).

1. The gate of inference (*anumāna*). 2. The gate of fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). 3. The gate of fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*). 4. The gate of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). 5. The gate of fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).
Furthermore, the first [the gate of inference] is divided into three parts: 1. A general presentation of the proof (*sādhana*); 2. A detailed explanation of the three members (*trirūpa*);
3. A conclusion establishing the thesis (*siddhārtha*). First, the general presentation of the proof:

In this context, the multiple statements consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth are called the "proof" (*sādhana*). This is because these multiple statements—thesis, reason, and example—reveal the meaning that has not yet been understood by those who inquire.

This means that within this "door of proof" (*sādhana*), the collection of many words consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) that are expressed without fault is called "proof.

Question: Why are three members required to constitute a proof? Answer: It is because only through the many words of the thesis, reason, and example can one fully reveal the meaning to those questioners who have not yet understood it.
That is to say, those questioners do not understand the fundamental nature of all phenomena.

Regarding the thesis of permanence, impermanence, and so forth, one remains hesitant and indecisive. The master of the treatise establishes a three-membered inference (trirūpa-anumāna) to cause [the opponent] to understand that the reason (*hetu*) is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), and that the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) serves as a clear instruction; thus, regarding the thesis of impermanence and so forth, one becomes clearly and spontaneously resolved.

Furthermore, the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) each possess multiple principles, which are termed "multiple statements" (*bahuvacana*). Within the thesis, there are nine such statements: first, non-contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

second, non-contradiction with inference (*anumāna*); third, non-contradiction with one’s own scriptures (*svaśāstra*); fourth, non-contradiction with worldly consensus (*loka*); fifth, non-contradiction with one’s own words (*svavacana*);
sixth, the complete establishment of the specific characteristics of the thesis itself; seventh, the [establishment of] the... [the object of the thesis].

1. The basis of the specific school (*pakṣāśraya*) is established through consensus (*prasiddha*). 2. Both the subject (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*) are established through consensus. 3. There is no contradiction with what is already established (*na pratyakṣaviruddha*).

Within the reason (*hetu*), there are three [qualifiers]: first, that which establishes (*sādhaka*); second, definitiveness (*niścaya*); and third, non-contradiction (*avirodha*). Regarding that which establishes, there are four types:

first, that which establishes for both parties (*ubhayasiddha*), because it is accepted by both the proponent and the opponent; second, that which establishes for either one (*anyatarasiddha*), because it is accepted even by the opponent.

Third, it is capable of establishing [the probandum] with certainty, because there is no doubt. Fourth, it is capable of establishing [the probandum] by way of its basis, because the property of existence is present.
There are six types of certainty: first, certainty that it is not common, because the reason is absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*);

second, certainty that it is not uncommon, because the reason is present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*); third, certainty that it does not occur in only a portion of the similar class, because it occurs throughout the dissimilar class.
4. It definitely does not occur as a partial occurrence within a dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). It is only admitted to occur pervasively within the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
5. It definitely does not occur as a partial occurrence within both classes. 6. It is definitely not contradictory. There are four types of non-contradiction:

(1) the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a reason that is not contradictory; (2) the specific differentiation (*viśeṣa*) of a reason that is not contradictory; (3) the reason that is not contradictory... [text fragment].

It contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*) that exists. Regarding the four reasons (*hetu*), they do not contradict the attributes (*viśeṣa*) of the existing subject.

Within the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there are two types of "many words" (*bahuvacana*): first, the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); second, the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). There are five aspects to the similar example: first, the similar example that establishes the reason; second, the similar example that establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*);
third, that which establishes both the thesis and the reason; fourth, the phrasing that coordinates the three members (*trirūpa*); fifth, the [concluding] statement.
Non-inverted conjunction. There are five types of dissimilar examples (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): first, a dissimilar example that can refute the thesis (*pakṣa*);

second, a dissimilar example that can refute the reason (*hetu*); third, one that can refute both the thesis and the reason; fourth, one where the three factors are separated by a negative particle (*nañ*); fifth, one where the negative particle is not inverted.
One should know that many such verbal expressions are all fallacies of reasoning; thus, these thirty-three fallacies are termed "pseudo-probants" (*sādhanābhāsa*). Conversely...
Excessive [reasoning] is also considered a principle; thus, thirty-three principles are called "true means of proof" (*sādhana*). Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:

"These many words are designated as 'means of proof' and 'pseudo-means of proof. According to their respective applications, these means of proof and pseudo-means of proof are explained for the purpose of enlightening others.
The first section, the general presentation of the means of proof, is concluded. Below, the second section provides a detailed explanation of the three members [of the syllogism].
This is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, the explanation of the reason (*hetu*); and third, the explanation of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

First, regarding the explanation of the thesis: herein, a "thesis" refers to that which is a well-established subject (*dharmin*) and a well-established predicate (*viśeṣaṇa*), characterized by their distinct natures;
it is that which one intends to establish according to one's own preference. This is called the thesis. For example: "Sound is impermanent."
Phenomena do not arise in isolation; they are produced only by relying upon objects. Whenever a thesis is established, one must first present a phenomenon as the basis of that thesis (*pakṣāśraya*).
Since there is no fault within this phenomenon, it is called a "thoroughly established subject" (*prasiddhadharmin*). One then investigates whether this phenomenon is true or false.

"Permanence," "impermanence," and so forth are established as the thesis (*pakṣa*). Because they can distinguish this dharma without error, they are called the "perfectly established qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Since the latter member of the thesis—the essence of the thesis—is the qualifier, the former member—the locus of the thesis—is the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
Furthermore, "thesis" (*pakṣa*) means "root," "guide," and "veneration. Establishing the thesis as the root guides and leads all other meanings.

Therefore, one esteems it. Thus, if one establishes "impermanence" as the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) must also be impermanent; if one establishes "permanence" as the thesis, the reason and the example must also be permanent.
This constitutes a faultless establishment of the thesis; hence it is said that the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is universally established (*prasiddha*).

Regarding the phrase "because of its differentiated nature, it is according to one's own preference": this means that within the subject (*dharmin*) of the preceding proposition, there is a sense of differentiation, which follows one's own [intention].
The intention is to take a single object as the thesis (*pakṣa*). For example, taking a jade stone as the subject (*dharmin*) presented before one, and establishing it as the basis for the thesis:
"The substance of the jade is hard" and "the color of the jade is white"—these constitute its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).
Within these specific qualities, one establishes "hardness" or "whiteness" according to one's own inclination; this nature that is established is what is called the thesis.
This explains the establishment of the nature of the thesis (*pakṣa*). That which is established is what is termed the "thesis.

It is called "that which is established" (*sādhya*) in contrast to the subsequent reason (*hetu*), because the thesis is that which is to be proven, while the reason is the means of proof. This means that although a thesis is proposed, its principle is not yet certain;

it must be established by adducing a reason for the meaning of the thesis to be finally settled. Therefore, the reason is the "means of establishment," and the thesis is the "object to be established."

This establishes [the definition]. Furthermore, he provides an example, saying: "For instance, if one posits 'sound' as the subject (*dharmin*) under discussion and 'impermanence' as the thesis (*pakṣa*), then because sound possesses arising and ceasing, it is necessarily impermanent by principle;
this is what constitutes 'universal consensus' (*prasiddha*). △ The first section, the explanation of the thesis, is complete. Below, the second section explains the reason (*hetu*).

The reason has three characteristics. What are these three? They are: being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), being necessarily present in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and being entirely absent in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*).
What are called "similar instances" and "dissimilar instances"? They refer to those categories that share the same logical status as the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
This is called the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*). For example, when establishing impermanence, things such as a jar are called similar instances because they are impermanent.

As for the "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*), it refers to those cases where that which is to be established is absent; for example, if something were permanent, one would observe that it is not produced, such as space and so forth.

In this context, the property of being produced, or the property of being produced immediately following volitional effort, is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and is invariably present in the similar instances.
The property of existence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and the complete absence of that property in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), constitute the reason for impermanence and so forth.
Since the reason is the nature of the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), the property of the thesis is taken as the reason. "Class" (*pakṣa*) is a name for all objects;

it refers to the three members [of the syllogism] collectively. The definite presence [in the similar class] and the universal absence [from the dissimilar class] together manifest the nature of the reason. That the reason has three characteristics means:

The "concordant" (*sapakṣa*) and "discordant" (*vipakṣa*) categories are the same as the "similar class" (*sādharmya-pakṣa*) and "dissimilar class" (*vaidharmya-pakṣa*). To say that [the reason] "pervades the nature of the property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharmatva*) is to reveal the meaning of the concordant class.
This is because the reason of the concordant class pervades only the thesis of the concordant class, and the reason of the discordant class pervades only the thesis of the discordant class;

this is what is called "pervading the nature of the property of the thesis. Therefore, Nāgārjuna takes "pervading the nature of the property of the thesis" to be the concordant class. Regarding the similar class...

"Being definitely present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and entirely absent in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)" means that the reason is definitely present in the similar class and is entirely absent within the dissimilar class;
because the reason of the similar class does not occur in the dissimilar class, this is free from fault. "How so? introduces the double interrogation.
"That which is... provides the specific explanation. The phrase "the property to be established" (*sādhyadharma*) refers to that which is to be proven.
The thesis (*pakṣa*) refers to the thesis and its reason (*hetu*), whose meanings are equal; this is the meaning of "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*). For example, as established below:
taking "impermanence" as the thesis and "jars and the like" as the example, because jars and the like possess the property of impermanence, they are called "similar instances.
This concludes the establishment of the thesis to be proven, as it is similar to the examples such as jars. Below, regarding "dissimilar instances" (*vipakṣa*), [it is distinguished separately].
Explaining the "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*). This refers to a locus where that which is to be established (*sādhya*) is absent;

that is, the locus of the reason (*hetu*) where the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) does not exist. If there were something eternal—meaning, if there were something to be established in the dissimilar instance—it would necessarily be an eternal phenomenon (*nityadharma*).
Therefore, the three members of the dissimilar instance are established as follows: "Eternality is the thesis," and "it is observed to be non-produced."

The reason (*hetu*) is, for example, like space and so forth. Because the thesis (*pakṣa*) of permanence is different from impermanence, and because the nature of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is different from that which is produced, and because the examples such as space are different from things such as jars, they are called the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Below this, the meaning of the reason is concluded.
As for the term "the nature of being produced," it refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*); these are of the nature of being produced through diligent and vigorous effort.

Because that which arises in the interval is also of the nature of being produced, it is "pervasive" (*vyāpin*). Regarding the phrase "pervasive of the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma-vyāpin*):

the aforementioned "nature of being produced" is a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) with respect to the thesis (*pakṣa*) of impermanence, and a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) with respect to the thesis of permanence; therefore, it is called "pervasive of the property of the subject."

Regarding "certainty of existence in the similar class (sapakṣa) and universal non-existence in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa)": the meaning is that if "impermanence" is the thesis (pakṣa), then the property of being produced exists in the similar class and is absent in the dissimilar class;
if "permanence" is the thesis, then the property of being produced is absent in the similar class and present in the dissimilar class.

Because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is pervasive throughout the similar class; because it exists in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it is pervasive throughout the dissimilar class.

Therefore, the treatise states that "impermanence and so forth" refers to the thesis of permanence; this concludes by demonstrating that this reason is pervasive throughout the similar class of the thesis of impermanence.

It is also entirely present in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) of the thesis (*pakṣa*). Therefore, it is said that "it is entirely the property of the thesis. △ Second, the explanation of the reason (*hetu*) is completed. Below, third, is the explanation of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
There are two kinds of examples: first, the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); second, the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the similar instance: where this is manifested—
The reason exists with certainty in the similar class (*sapakṣa*); that is to say, whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar and so forth.
As for the dissimilar property (*vipakṣa*), it is where the probandum is stated not to exist, and the reason is entirely absent;

that is to say, whatever is permanent is seen not to be produced, such as space and so forth. Herein, the word "permanent" indicates what is not impermanent, and the phrase "not produced" indicates its absence.
Regarding what is produced: that which exists as if it were non-existent is called "non-existent.

As for "the same dharma" (*ekadharma*): "dharma" refers to both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*). The basis of the thesis is called the "subject" (*dharmī*), while the essence of the thesis is simply called "dharma.

The reason is called a "thesis-dharma" (*pakṣadharma*); therefore, both the thesis and the reason are termed "dharma. Because the example must necessarily share the same "similar class" (*sapakṣa*) as the thesis and the reason, it is so named.
"Similarity of nature" (*sādharmya*). Regarding the "two dissimilarities of nature" (*vaidharmya*): this refers to the example of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Although it shares the same thesis (*pakṣa*) and reason (*hetu*) as the dissimilar class, it must necessarily differ from the properties of the similar class (*sapakṣa*); therefore, it is called "dissimilarity of nature.

As for the section beginning with "Similarity of nature," it explains the meaning of the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). "In this place" refers to the locus of the similar example. "Manifesting the reason in the similar class" means manifesting the [reason] that is present in the similar class.

The reason for establishing [the thesis] is the same as the example. "Having a determined presence" means that within the similar example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*), there is the determined presence of the nature of the reason (*hetutva*) in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). To provide an illustration: by means of the reason "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*).
Observing that thesis of impermanence, one employs examples such as a jar. The section "The dissimilar property" below explains the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
"In this place" refers to the locus of the dissimilar example. "The probandum is absent" means that the thesis to be established is not present in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
"The reason is entirely non-existent" means that the reason present in the similar instances is entirely absent from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

Because [the reason] exists [in the dissimilar class], another dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is established as follows: "If 'being permanent' is the thesis (*pakṣa*), then 'not being produced by effort' (*akṛtaka*) is the reason, and 'such as space' (*ākāśādivat*) is the example.
In this context, the meaning of how the dissimilar class differs from the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is not explained.
This means that within this dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), the term "the thesis of permanence" indicates that it is not the same as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)—the thesis of impermanence.

The term "not being produced" indicates that there is no cause which is "produced" within the similar instance. As for the phrase "just as," it provides an example to explain and establish the meaning of the similar and dissimilar instances.
That is to say, just as where there is existence, there must be non-existence; the word "existence" refers to the similar instance, while "non-existence" refers to...
The dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Because the meaning of "being present in the similar instance" does not apply within the dissimilar instance, the dissimilar instance is said to be "non-existent.

Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "In contrast to the theory of existence, 'existence' refers to the similar instance; in contrast to the theory of non-existence, it refers to the dissimilar instance. △ The third section, the explanation of the example, is concluded.
This completes the two preceding sections on the detailed explanation of the three members [of the syllogism]. Below follows the third section: the conclusion.

Regarding the establishment of the thesis (*sādhana*): when one employs such multiple statements as the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and so forth, in order to enlighten another, these are called the "means of proof" (*sādhana*).

For example, the statement "sound is impermanent" is the expression of the thesis; "because it is produced" is the expression of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); and "if it is produced... [is the application].
"Seeing that it is impermanent, like a jar and so forth," is a statement of similarity (*anvaya*).
"If it were permanent, it would be seen as non-produced, like space," is a statement of exclusion (*vyatireka*). These three parts alone are designated as the "means of proof" (*sādhana*).

Below, the second section explains "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
There are six types of inconclusive [reasons]: first, the common; second, the uncommon; third, that which occurs in a portion of the similar class but pervades the dissimilar class;
fourth, that which occurs in a portion of the dissimilar class but pervades the similar class; fifth, that which occurs in portions of both classes; and sixth, the contradictory indecisive.
In summary, there are six types of fallacies of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The following text provides a detailed explanation of each one.

Among these, the "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) is as follows: for example, if one says, "Sound is eternal because it is an object of cognition," this reason is common to both the class of the eternal and the class of the non-eternal.
Therefore, it is inconclusive: is sound impermanent because it is an object of cognition, like a jar and so forth?
Or is sound permanent because it is an object of cognition, like space and so forth?
First, [the author] explains the fallacy of the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) of the common reason (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*). For example, one might state: "Sound is the subject (*dharmin*);
it is permanent (*nitya*), because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*). Here, having first stated the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be proven and the reason (*hetu*), he then points out the fallacy:

"Both the class of the permanent (*nitya-pakṣa*) and the class of the impermanent (*anitya-pakṣa*) share this reason; therefore, it is inconclusive. This is because the reason, "being an object of cognition," applies to the permanent...

The thesis (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), as well as the thesis and example of impermanence, are all "common" (*sādhāraṇa*). To explain the meaning of "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntika*), it is as follows:
[Is sound] like a jar and so forth, because of its being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), such that the property-bearer (*dharmin*)—sound—is the thesis of impermanence?

Since those jars have various sizes, depths, and so on, yet are all objects of cognition; or is it like space and so forth, because of its being an object of cognition, such that [the example] is sound?
There is a thesis: "The subject is eternal," because that space can be measured in terms of distance, proximity, direction, and shape.

This reason—namely, "because it possesses the nature of being measurable"—is too broad (*asādhāraṇa*), as it is common to both the class of the eternal and the class of the non-eternal; thus, it constitutes a logical fallacy.

Regarding the term "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*): it is as when one says, "Sound is eternal, because it possesses the nature of being audible. This reason is excluded from both the class of the eternal and the class of the non-eternal;
since nothing else exists outside of the eternal and the non-eternal, this is a reason for doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*). What, then, is this "nature of being audible" like?

The second [section] explains the fallacy of the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*) that is not shared with the opponent. "Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*). "It is necessarily permanent" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
"Because it is audible" is the reason (*hetu*). Herein, having stated the thesis and the reason, the inconclusiveness is further demonstrated as follows:

both the class of the permanent and the class of the impermanent are devoid of this reason—namely, audibility. That is to say, audibility is absent from both the permanent example for the thesis and the example for the impermanent.

Therefore, why is this? [If one argues: "Like a jar and so forth, sound is not of the nature of being audible"—this is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the subject (*dharmin*) "sound," and the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is impermanent (*anitya*).
Or, "Like space and so forth, sound is not of the nature of being audible"—this is the example for the subject "sound," and the thesis is that it is permanent (*nitya*).
Since both the jar and space are visible by the eye, they are not of the nature of being audible; therefore, they are distinct. Apart from permanence and impermanence, there is nothing else.
"Because it exists" indicates the meaning of being indeterminate (*anaikāntika*). "The nature of what is heard" indicates the meaning of being unique (*asādhāraṇa*). What, then, is this like?
It is to clarify the meaning of its uniqueness.

Regarding that which occurs in one part of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) but occurs throughout the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*): for example, it is said, "Sound is not produced immediately following volitional effort, because it is impermanent.
In this case, the thesis (*pakṣa*)—"not produced immediately following volitional effort"—has lightning and space as its similar class.
This property of impermanence exists in lightning and so forth, but does not exist in space and so forth. It is not [produced] immediately following volitional effort...
Establishing the thesis: taking jars and the like as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), this reason is present in all of them.

Since this reason—namely, being produced by effort—is a property shared with both lightning and jars (the similar instances), it is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance, just as jars and the like are impermanent and yet are produced by effort, so too might lightning be impermanent and yet not be produced by effort;
or conversely, just as lightning is impermanent and not produced by effort, so too might jars and the like be impermanent and yet be produced by effort.

The three explanations are identical regarding the fallacy of the reason occurring in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) while occurring throughout all dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

As stated below, the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) are established: "That which is not produced by immediate volitional effort" is the thesis; "because it is impermanent" is the reason. In the section beginning with "In this regard," the thesis is restated and an example is cited.
In the section beginning with "This impermanence," it clarifies that the reason incurs the fallacy of not occurring in one part of the example, using lightning as the illustration.

Impermanence occurs through dependence on causes. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is permanent because it lacks causes. "Not produced by volitional effort" (*aprayatnāntarīyaka*) is a restatement of the same thesis (*pakṣa*) citing a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
"Pervasive in that" indicates that both the reason (*hetu*) and the jar (*ghaṭa*) are impermanent; this is the meaning of "pervasive occurrence.
"This reason," etc., demonstrates the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*); namely, that the two examples—the flash of lightning and the jar—are identical in this regard.

Because it is a phenomenon subject to impermanence (*anitya*). It is as follows: in the section explaining the application of the reason and the example, the meaning of "indefiniteness" (*anaikāntika*) is clarified.
That is to say, the example of a jar and so forth—which is impermanent—is a product of volitional effort (*prayatnāntarīyaka*).

Because it possesses the property of impermanence, which is the reason, it establishes the thesis for the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), namely that [sound] is a product of volitional effort, just like lightning and so forth.

The analogy of "impermanence" [as a reason]—namely, "because it is not produced by uninterrupted effort and possesses the nature of impermanence"—is able to establish the thesis within the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
However, since the reason "not produced by uninterrupted effort" implies impermanence, the reason is too broad;

it commits the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to both the similar and dissimilar classes (*vipakṣa*), because it applies to a place where it ought not to apply, namely, the dissimilar class.
If it were to occur pervasively in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), yet only partially in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), would this not be a fallacy?
For instance, consider the thesis: "Sound is produced by immediate effort, because it is impermanent.
Here, the similar class for the thesis "produced by immediate effort" consists of things such as pots. Its...

The nature of impermanence is present everywhere in this [subject]. Taking lightning, space, and so forth as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), it exists in some parts of them—such as lightning—and is absent in others—such as space.
Therefore, as before, it remains inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Fourth, the refutation of the fallacy that [the reason] occurs in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) while occurring throughout all similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Below this, the outline is restated and introduced.
As established below, the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) are stated: "The thesis is that [sound] is produced by immediate effort; the reason is 'because it has the nature of impermanence'.
Below the phrase "produced by immediate effort," the thesis is restated and an example is cited: as for this nature of impermanence, in this regard...
"Pervasive existence" (*vyāpti*) indicates that the reason coexists with the similar instances; this is the meaning of "pervasive occurrence. The passage beginning with "like lightning, space, etc.

cites examples from dissimilar instances to demonstrate the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). That is to say, regarding the reason "because of being impermanent," it is said to exist when it is associated with lightning and so forth, as they possess the nature of impermanence;
yet it is said to be absent when associated with space and so forth, as they possess the nature of permanence. Therefore...
As before, because lightning and the jar are taken as having the same property (*sādharmya*), this too is an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason;
for it does not apply to one part of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), namely, to lightning.
Regarding that which occurs in one part of both [similar and dissimilar instances]: for example, it is said that "sound is permanent because it lacks material resistance.

Herein, the thesis of permanence takes space (*ākāśa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth as its similar instances (*sapakṣa*). The property of lacking material resistance exists in space and so forth, but does not exist in atoms and so forth.
It takes jars (*ghaṭa*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth as its dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); it exists in pleasure and so forth, but does not exist in jars and so forth. Therefore, this reason—
Because pleasure and emptiness are taken as having the same property (*sādharmya*), this is also called "indeterminate" (*anaikāntika*).

It is explained as the fallacy of the reason (*hetu*) occurring in only one part of both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). Regarding the term "both classes," it means that the reason occurs in only one part of each, namely the similar and the dissimilar classes.
For example, in the statement, "Sound is eternal because it lacks resistance (*apratighāta*)," the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) are established. By...

"Permanence" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). "Lack of material obstruction" is the reason (*hetu*). Herein, the section beginning with "In this regard, below" restates the thesis and cites an analogy to establish the thesis of permanence:

the nature of space is permanent, and atoms (*paramāṇu*) are also permanent; these are suitable as similar instances (*sapakṣa*). The section beginning with "Lack of material obstruction, below" explains the meaning of the reason's partial occurrence within the similar instances.
That is to say, because the reason—"due to the lack of material obstruction"—applies to space, which lacks material obstruction, it is stated as follows:
There are atoms that possess material obstruction; these are said to be "non-existent" [in the context of permanence].

If one takes jars, pleasure, and so forth as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), then since jars and the like are impermanent, and suffering and pleasure are likewise not permanent, it would be appropriate to take them as examples for the dissimilar instances when establishing the thesis of permanence within the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Regarding the statement that [the reason] exists in pleasure and the like, but does not exist in a jar and the like, this explains the meaning of "occurring in only one part of the dissimilar class" (*vipakṣaikadeśavṛtti*).

That is to say, with respect to the reason "because it lacks material resistance": since pleasure lacks material resistance, it is said to exist; whereas since a jar possesses material resistance, it is said not to exist.
Therefore, the following concludes that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding the "contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*): for example, one might establish the thesis that "sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot," while another establishes that "sound is permanent because it is audible, like the nature of sound.
Since both of these are reasons for doubt, they are both termed "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
Sixth, the fallacy of the "contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). To speak of "contradictory certainty" is simply "certainty in contradiction.
This phrasing originates from the translators; while the wording is inverted, the meaning remains consistent. Thus, the *Zongjing lu* (Mirror of the Source) commentary states:

"Now, the fallacy of 'uncertainty due to contradictory certainty' occurs when the proponent and opponent both dispute a single *dharmin* (subject), yet their respective reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*udāharaṇa*) differ, each possessing the three characteristics (*trairūpya*), and both are pervasive [in the subject]."

The property of being the subject (*pakṣadharma*), its necessary presence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and its universal absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*) merely fail to produce correct cognition in one another;
because both parties remain in doubt, they cannot definitively establish a single thesis. This is termed the "inconclusive fallacy of contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).

As established above, the three branches [of the syllogism] were set forth. As established below, the three branches are again set forth. The phrase "these two" below demonstrates the fallacy of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding the term "contradictory": "eternal" (*nitya*) and "non-eternal" (*anitya*) are contradictory in meaning. Since these two are contradictory, they function as both similar and dissimilar instances (*sapakṣa* and *vipakṣa*) for one another.
When "eternal" is the thesis (*pakṣa*), "non-eternal" is the dissimilar instance; when "non-eternal" is the thesis, "eternal" is the dissimilar instance.
Regarding "certainty" (*niścaya*): it consists in establishing two theses (*pakṣa*), each possessing three members (*avayava*) and all possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*).

This constitutes certainty. That is to say: the reason (*hetu*) present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) must pervade the entire similar class; the reason present in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) must pervade the entire dissimilar class—this is what is meant by "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Furthermore, the reason present in the similar class must not occur in the dissimilar class; this is its "necessary presence" (*sattva*) in the similar class.
The nature [of the reason] is such that it does not occur in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), yet it is entirely absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Although both schools may present this argument, it cannot be definitively established regarding a single factual basis (*dharmin*); to state it thus is considered a fault. △ Second, the explanation of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reason is finished.
Below, third, is the explanation of the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) reason.

There are four types of contradiction: namely, the contradictory reason regarding the intrinsic nature of the property (*dharma-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*), the contradictory reason regarding the specific qualification of the property (*dharma-viśeṣa-viruddha-hetu*), the contradictory reason regarding the intrinsic nature of the locus (*dharmin-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*), and the contradictory reason regarding the specific qualification of the locus (*dharmin-viśeṣa-viruddha-hetu*), and so forth.
In summary, there are four types of fallacies involving contradiction (*viruddha*). The following text explains each one individually.
Among these, the "reason contradictory with the specific characteristic of the property" (*dharmasvalakṣaṇaviruddhahetu*) is as follows:

for example, to say that sound is permanent because it is produced (*kṛtakatvāt*), or because it is produced by immediate effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatvāt*). This reason exists only in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); therefore, it is contradictory.
First, the explanation of the fallacy of the contradictory reason (*dharmasvalakṣaṇaviruddhahetu*). Regarding "the self-characteristic of the property" (*dharmasvalakṣaṇa*):

this refers to the fact that all phenomena each possess their own specific characteristic, which is the very essence of the thesis (*pakṣa*) being established. Regarding "contradictory" (*viruddha*): this means that the reason contradicts the thesis.
For example, if one says, "Because it is produced by immediate volitional effort," how could this establish the thesis of a permanent entity that is not produced? As it is said:
Below, the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) are established: "Eternal" is the thesis;
"because it is a product" (*kṛtakatvāt*), or "because it is produced by volitional effort without interruption," is the reason. Below this, the reason is restated to reveal its fallacy:

if the thesis is that it is eternal and its nature is not a product, then the reason "because it is a product" exists only in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) of the non-eternal; therefore, it is [inconclusive].
Contradictory. Because all things that are impermanent are produced by causes.

Regarding the reason that contradicts the specific characteristic of a phenomenon (*dharmaviśeṣaviparītahetu*): as when it is said that the eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another because they possess the nature of being an accumulation, like bedding and so forth.
Just as this reason can establish that the eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another, so too can it [establish the opposite].

[This establishes] the contradiction regarding the distinction between the property and the locus of the property (*dharmin*). Regarding the bedding and other items used by others for the purpose of collective enjoyment by others:

secondly, [it concerns] the fault of the contradictory reason regarding the distinction of the property (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddhahetu*). As for what is called the "contradictory reason regarding the distinction of the property," these are all...
In this doctrine, the reason for establishing a distinction cannot be proven; it is said to be contradictory. As stated below, the three members [of the syllogism] are established:

taking the five faculties, such as the eye, as the subject (*dharmin*), "they must exist for the sake of another" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); "because they possess the nature of being an accumulation" is the reason (*hetu*);
and "like bedding and so forth" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Since the eye and other faculties do not function for their own sake, they must [exist for the sake of another]. The eye...
Since the various consciousnesses function as their basis, the thesis is established that they must exist for the sake of another.

Furthermore, the sense organs such as the eye are fundamentally composed of the eight factors—earth, water, fire, wind, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—and thus possess the nature of an accumulation.

Therefore, by taking this nature of accumulation as the reason, it is shown that because they are produced by a multitude of conditions such as bedding and other requisites, they too must exist for the sake of another.

Therefore, it is stated as an analogy. "This cause," and so forth, restates the reason to establish the thesis. "In this way," and so forth, reveals the fault of the contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) regarding the specific characteristics of the phenomena.
In my observation of the interpretations of various schools concerning the meaning of this chapter, all cite the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (Seventy Verses on Sāṃkhya) as their proof.
The phrasing of both [positions] is vague and their elucidation is not yet thorough, causing students to view this matter with uncertainty.
Now, let us clarify it through the principle of the three aspects (*trirūpa*); thus, the meaning seems clearer. Let me explain further. Regarding the "differentiation of phenomena" (*dharma-viśeṣa*):

taking the sense organs such as the eye as the subject (*dharmin*) under discussion, one establishes [the proposition] because the meaning of the "organ" (*indriya*) possesses differentiation. The thesis...
The dharmas also possess distinctions. The *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) is the basis for the visual consciousness and other cognitions;

the *darśanabhāga* (perceptual aspect) is that which is produced by the visual faculty and other organs. Since the objective and perceptual aspects are distinct, it is said that the eye is a self-aggregate that must necessarily be utilized by another cognition.
Thus, the thesis is established: "It must necessarily be used by another. Furthermore, the objective and perceptual aspects [are] for oneself...

Regarding the function of the *sākṣātkāra-bhāga* (the aspect of direct realization): its *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (the aspect of self-realization) constitutes the substance (*ātman*) of the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect) and the *darśana-bhāga* (the subjective aspect). As substance, it maintains its own functional activity;

this activity does not exist for the sake of another. Furthermore, a thesis is established: "It certainly does not exist for the sake of another. Therefore, the specific characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the phenomena (*dharmin*), such as the eye-faculties and so forth, are designated as existing for the sake of another.
That which exists for the sake of another and that which certainly does not exist for the sake of another are termed the "qualifications" (*viśeṣa*) of the phenomenon (*dharma*). Now...

Because it possesses the nature of being an accumulation, it serves as a reason (*hetu*). This corresponds to the analogy of bedding and so forth. It establishes only the thesis (*pakṣa*) that [the eyes, etc. must exist for the sake of another;
it cannot establish the thesis that they must not exist for the sake of another. Therefore, this reason contradicts the qualified thesis (*viśeṣya-pakṣa*). Thus, the treatise states:
"If this reason were able to establish that the eyes and so forth must necessarily exist for the sake of another, then even if one were to grant its establishment..."
Regarding the phrase "a portion of the meaning within the thesis": this also demonstrates that one can establish a distinction within the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
It shows that there is likewise a portion of the meaning consisting of a distinction within the thesis, which should also be capable of being established by means of the reason (*hetu*).

However, it is stated [that this is not the case] because a thesis that is not intended for another’s sake and a thesis intended for another’s sake are mutually contradictory when combined with a cumulative reason. Therefore, it says:

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, it is said that bedding and other such items are for the collective use and enjoyment by others," this explains that both the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are for the sake of others.
Therefore, within the thesis (*pakṣa*), there must necessarily be a distinction in one part: the characteristic of not being for the sake of others is contradictory [to the reason].
There is a reason that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a property (*dharma*). For example, it is said:

"Existence (*sattā*) is not a substance (*dravya*), nor a quality (*guṇa*), nor an action (*karman*), because it possesses [the universal] existence, and because it possesses qualities and actions, just like the category of generality (*sāmānyatva*).

This reason, while being able to establish the negation of substance and so forth, likewise establishes the negation of existence itself, because both [the probandum and the negation] are equally certain.
Third, there is the fallacy of the contradictory reason (*svabhāvaviruddha-hetu*) regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*).

"The specific characteristic of the subject" refers to the specific characteristic of the locus of the thesis (*pakṣadharmin*) as it was previously stated. It is called "contradictory" because the reason fails to establish the specific characteristic of the subject;

thus, it is termed "contradictory. This originates from the Vaiśeṣika school’s doctrine of the six categories (*ṣatpadārtha*), wherein the fourth category is the category of "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*), which [pervades] substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and...

There are three types of action (*karman*). Because they share the same existence (*sattā*), there exists a distinct category as their essence apart from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).

It is by virtue of this Great Existence (*mahāsattā*) that substances and so forth exist. What is here called "the nature of existence" (*sattā-jāti*) is precisely that category-meaning of Great Existence (*mahāsattā-pada-artha*), as will be explained below.
The three members [of the syllogism] are established as follows: taking "the nature of existence" (*sattā*) as the subject (*pakṣa*) of the initial proposition.

Because this nature of existence exists as a distinct substantial entity apart from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*), it is stated that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is: "It is neither substance, nor quality, nor action.

Furthermore, because this nature of existence is originally one and the same "existence" shared by the triad of substance, quality, and action, it is stated: "Because there is one substance, there is a quality."

Action (*karman*) serves as the cause. Furthermore, this existence (*sattā*) is similar by virtue of possessing real qualities and actions (*guṇa-karman*), and it is dissimilar by virtue of not possessing unreal qualities and actions.

Therefore, it is said that "similarity" and "dissimilarity" serve as the metaphors. Below this, the reason (*hetu*) is restated to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*) and to reveal the fault of contradiction (*viruddha-doṣa*).
That is to say, by means of reasons such as "there being one reality," a thesis such as "not being a reality" is established; does this not constitute a mutual exclusion? Therefore...

The phrase "clouds obstruct" and so forth refers to the thesis that [entities] are not non-real and so on. As follows: this demonstrates how the reason, through its successive application, contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*).

That is to say, when the reason "there is one real entity" and so on obstructs the thesis that they are not non-real and so on, then within the subject there is also the sense of being non-real and so on;
would this not also be obstructed? Therefore, it is said: "In this way, it is also capable of establishing an obstruction."

Regarding the phrase "because both [the existence of the property] and the non-reality within that existence are determined": this means that both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*) are contradictory with the reason (*hetu*), because both are determined.
Regarding the reason that contradicts the specific qualification of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddhahetu*): it is as follows.

This very same reason, with respect to the specific qualification of the subject in the aforementioned thesis, establishes the state of being an object of cognition (*sālambanatva*), yet it is also capable of establishing its opposite—the state of not being an object of cognition (*anālambanatva*). This is because, as in the case of negating [the category of] "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth, both [contradictory predicates] are equally determined.
Fourth, the fallacy of the contradictory reason regarding the qualification of the subject (*dharmin-viśeṣa-viruddha-hetu*) is explained.

"Qualification of the subject" refers to the sense that there is a distinction in the basis of the thesis (*pakṣadharmin*) as presented previously. "Contradictory" means that the reason is unable to establish that qualified meaning.
As follows below, the reason is cited to establish the subject; that very reason is the aforementioned reason, "because it exists as a single reality," and so forth.

Regarding the distinction of the *dharmin* (the subject) within the preceding thesis: it refers to the distinction between "reality" (*sat*) and "qualities, actions, and substances" (*guṇa-karma-dravya*) within the aforementioned nature of existence (*mahāsattā*).

As for being "that which has existence as its object" (*sālambana*), it means that by means of the reason "because there is reality" (*sat-tvāt*), one establishes the nature of "having reality" (*sat-sattā*);
this is called "having existence as its object. Furthermore, the phrase "it can also [establish]" below explains the meaning of contradiction, namely, "there is [existence]."

The cause, such as "being real" (*sat*), can establish one part of the subject (*dharmin*)—namely, that it is "real"—and it can also establish another part that is contrary to this "being real," namely, that it is "not real.

Since the presence of the cause "being real" establishes a subject that is "not real," it functions as a non-existent condition (*abhāva-pratyaya*). If it is not an existent condition, then "being real" [is established].
The reasons such as "reality" (*satya*) cannot establish the absence of reality within the subject (*dharmin*), nor can they establish the presence of reality within the subject.
Therefore, it is said that this is like the negation of reality and so forth, because both are equally determined.

That is to say, just as in the previous chapter the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the subject were both negated, so too are these two distinct meanings within the subject. △ Third, the explanation of contradiction.

Having already explained pseudo-reasons, we shall now explain pseudo-examples. There are five types of pseudo-examples based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*): first, the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*).

There are five types [of fallacious examples]: first, the unestablished; second, the unestablished thesis-property; third, the unestablished in both respects; fourth, the lack of connection; and fifth, the inverted connection.

There are likewise five types of fallacious examples based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*): first, the failure to exclude the thesis-property; second, the failure to exclude the probans; and third, the failure to exclude both.
Four are non-separation; five are inverted separation.

Having already explained the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) previously, the fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) to be discussed hereafter are introduced. There are five faults each for the fallacious example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) and the fallacious example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*);
these are termed "fallacious examples. These will be explained individually in the following text. △ First, concluding the previous section and providing a general heading.
