First, regarding the five types of fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), the first is that in which the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) is unestablished. For example, one might say: "Sound is eternal because it lacks resistance;

whatever lacks resistance is seen to be eternal, just like atoms (*paramāṇu*). However, in the case of those atoms, while the property to be established—eternality—is present, the property that establishes it [the reason] is not.
If one posits that there is no resistance [in atoms], it is because all atoms possess the nature of resistance.
One interpretation is that this is similar to the fault of the unestablished probans (*asiddha-hetu*) within the dharma and the example;

since the reason (*hetu*) is the property to be established and the example does not apply to that reason, it is called "unestablished. As stated below, the thesis and the reason are established by defining them as "permanent."

Thesis: Because they lack material obstruction (*sapratigha*), [atoms are eternal]. "All those that are not... and so forth: this restates the reason and the thesis, citing an example to establish the synthesis.

However, "But those... and so forth: this restates the example to reveal the fault. That is to say, while the nature of atoms is eternal—thus the property of eternity exists within the thesis to be established—and atoms possess material obstruction—thus the property of lacking material obstruction is absent from the reason used to establish it—it is therefore said, "by means of all atoms... [and so on].
"Subtle. Because its nature is that of material obstruction, the property to be established is not proven; that is to say, it is asserted to be like cognition (*buddhi*).

However, in all cognitions, while the property used for proof—the absence of material obstruction—exists, the property to be established—permanence—does not exist, because all cognitions are impermanent.
The second explanation is similar [to the first] regarding the fault of the unestablished thesis (*asiddha*) within the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is the property to be established;

since the example does not apply to the thesis, it is called "unestablished. This refers to stating, for instance, "like cognition" (*buddhi*), which cites an example to correspond with the preceding thesis and reason.
That is to say, taking "permanence" as the thesis and "lack of resistance" (*apratighāta*) as the reason, "like cognition" is given as the example. However, [the phrase] "but all... [below].
The fallacy is exposed by citing the analogy: "all cognition" refers to the mind of conceptualization and arising-and-ceasing.
Since the nature of cognition is unimpeded, it exists within the probans (*hetu*) as something non-obstructive;
yet since the nature of cognition is impermanent, it is absent from the probandum (*sādhya*) of an eternal nature. Therefore, it is said: "because all cognition is impermanent."
Regarding the non-establishment of both, there are again two types: existence and non-existence. If one says it is like a jar in terms of existence, both are unestablished.
If one speaks of it as being like space in relation to non-existence, both are likewise unestablished.
The three explanations are essentially the same regarding the fault of both the subject (*dharmin*) and the predicate (*dharma*) being unestablished in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

This means that the example cannot be applied to either the thesis (*pakṣa*) or the reason (*hetu*); this is called "unestablished for both. Furthermore, there are two types: "existent" and "non-existent.

These distinguish between the two sections of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). That which is "existent" refers to the similar instance, and that which is "non-existent" refers to the dissimilar instance. This refers to the aforementioned [subject].
In the *Liumen* (Establishment of the Gate), it says: "That which is like existence yet is not existence is called non-existence. This is where the text originates.

If one says "like a jar," this is an attempt to cite an analogy that matches the previous subject (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and similar instances (*sapakṣa*). To point out the fault when both [the reason and the example] are unestablished (*asiddha*):

it means that while the essence of a jar is impermanent, this contradicts the previous thesis (*sādhya*) of permanence; and while a jar possesses material obstruction (*sapratigha*), this contradicts the previous [thesis] of being without material substance.

The obstructing cause (*bādhaka-hetu*) is not established. Since "existence" (*sat*) is identical to the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), it is said that both [the example and the reason] are unestablished;
for the example of a jar and so forth is unestablished with respect to both the similar instance and the thesis-reason (*pakṣa-hetu*).

If one were to say "like space" in response to a proponent of non-existence (*asat-vādin*), this would cite an example that conforms to the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) rather than the thesis-reason. This is because the previous "eternal" thesis would have the "non-eternal" as its dissimilar instance. Thus, they are the same.

The reason for the similar class (sapakṣa) is that it is without material obstruction; the reason for the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is that it possesses material obstruction. To say "like space" [as an example]:

since the nature of space is permanent, it does not establish the thesis of the dissimilar class, which is impermanent. Since the nature of space is unobstructed, it does not establish the reason of the dissimilar class, which is obstructed.
That which is not existent is non-existent, and non-existence is the dissimilar class. Therefore, it is said that neither is established.
Because the analogy of space is unestablished for both the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) and the thesis-reason (*pakṣa-hetu*), there is no application (*upanaya*).

This means that in such a case, there is no joining together; rather, both the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) are manifested simultaneously in things such as a jar, as when one says:
"In a jar, we perceive the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and the property of impermanence (*anityatva*)."

The fourfold explanation [serves] to show that there is no fault of lacking the *upanaya* (application) term within the *dṛṣṭānta* (example). Specifically, in the passage beginning "That is to say, below," it establishes the definitive presence of the three members (*trirūpa*).
In the passage beginning "As for the statement below," it clarifies the absence of the *upanaya* term as a way of exposing the fault.

This means that although the method of formulating a formal inference (*prayoga*) possesses the three members, it must necessarily include both the *upanaya* and *nigamana* (conclusion) terms to constitute the patterns for the similar (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar (*vipakṣa*) cases. Furthermore, the *upanaya* must invariably precede the *pratijñā* (thesis).
In the *vyatireka* (negative) formulation, the thesis (*pakṣa*) comes first and the reason (*hetu*) follows. Since the reason is the means of establishing [the thesis], it is placed first;
since the thesis is that which is to be established, it follows next. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) serves as the illustrative instruction for the thesis and the reason, and thus it follows after them.
Now, although within the similar class (*sapakṣa*) there are examples such as a pot, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is the reason and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) is—
Thesis: To lack the formal structure of the "conjunction" (upanaya) constitutes a logical fallacy.
Regarding the "inverted conjunction": it refers to stating, "Whatever is produced is impermanent," yet inverting this to say, "Whatever is impermanent is produced."

The fifth explanation is similar to the fault of inverting the *upanaya* (application) within the simile; that is, while the term for the application should properly appear below, it appears above, thereby demonstrating the fault of an inverted application.

This concludes the section on fallacious similar-positive examples (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), wherein the five types of faults within fallacious similar-positive examples are established. △ The five types of similar-positive examples are completed above; below follow the five types of dissimilar-negative examples (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Regarding the case where that which is established in a "dissimilar instance" (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) is not excluded: for example, suppose one says, "All impermanent things are seen to possess resistance, like atoms.
Because the atom is established as being permanent, the property to be proven—impermanence—is not excluded [from the atom];
furthermore, the proving property—lack of resistance—is absent [in the atom]. Thus, it is a fallacy.
First, this explains the fault that the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*) fails to exclude what has been established [in the thesis]. "To exclude" (*vyāvṛtti*) means to distance oneself from.

That is to say, a dissimilar example must necessarily be distant from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), which consists of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*); this constitutes the essence of a dissimilar example. Since it does not exclude [the reason] here, it is stated as a fault.
Furthermore, as shown below, the term indicating separation is fixed: if there were separation, the thesis would come first and the reason afterwards; therefore [it is a fault].
It begins with the thesis of impermanence, followed by the reason of material obstruction, and then the example of the atom (*paramāṇu*).

Because of the latter, the example is cited below to reveal the fault: namely, that the nature of the atom is permanent, and thus it does not exclude the property to be proven—the thesis of permanence—within the aforementioned similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Therefore, it is said: "Because he establishes the atom as being of a permanent nature, the [reason] of material obstruction is capable of excluding [the thesis]."

In the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is no reason of non-obstructiveness; therefore it is said: "Where there is no non-obstructiveness, there is [no probandum]. Here, "non-existence" (*abhāva*) has the sense of exclusion (*apoha*).

Regarding the statement that "the prover (*sādhana*) is not excluded," this refers to the claim that, for example, like karma, one merely excludes the probandum (*sādhya*) but does not exclude the prover.
That is to say, they assert that all karmas are non-obstructive.
The second [point] concerns the fault that the probans (*sādhana*) is not excluded from the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), which appears to differ slightly from the formal explanation.

That is to say, when it is stated, "like karma," this cites an example to demonstrate the fault by aligning it with the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and similar class (*sapakṣa*). Since the nature of karma is impermanent, it possesses the sense of being "removed" from the previously established thesis of permanence within the similar class;
therefore, it is said that "only the probandum (*sādhyadharma*) is excluded. Furthermore, since the nature of karma is unimpeded, it does not exist within the similar class.
Because the characteristics of substantial obstruction and cause are mutually concordant, it is said that the probans (*sādhana*) is not refuted.
As for "both being unrefuted," this is stated in contrast to those who maintain [the existence of] entities, using the example of space (*ākāśa*).

This is because space does not refute its own nature of permanence and its nature of being without substantial obstruction; for space is described as being permanent and without substantial obstruction.
The third [type of] fallacious example shares the fault of failing to exclude both the subject (*dharmin*) and the predicate (*dharma*) from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

"Failing to exclude both" means that the dissimilar instance is concordant with the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) found within the similar instance (*sapakṣa*); this is termed "failing to exclude both.

Regarding the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* that "it is like space," "existence" (*sattva*) is the similar instance; this is cited as an example in conjunction with the preceding similar instance's thesis and reason. Because...

The following passage points out the fallacy: [the opponent] asserts that the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is permanent, yet does not exclude the property of permanence from its similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

They assert that the nature of emptiness is non-obstructive, yet do not exclude the reason of non-obstruction from its similar instances. Therefore, it is said: "Because [you] state that space (*ākāśa*) is of a permanent nature, and because it is without material obstruction."
Regarding "non-separation" (*aviyoga*): it refers to the statement, for example, that a jar possesses the nature of impermanence and the nature of resistance.
In the four types of explanations, there is no fault of lacking the term "separation" (*viyoga*) within the illustration of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

The method of establishing a formal inference (*prayoga*) requires that the combined members of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) must necessarily include the term "separation" to manifest the mode of the dissimilar instance. Now, however, there is only the name of the three members [of the syllogism] regarding the dissimilar instance; it is deficient.
Regarding the separation of words (*vyañjana-vyatireka*), it is considered a fault when they do not conform to the proper rules.
An inverted separation (*viparyasta-vyatireka*) refers, for example, to saying: "Whatever is characterized by resistance is all impermanent."
Fifth, the explanation of the fault of inverting the particle of exclusion (*vyatireka*) within the pseudo-dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
According to the rules of *hetuvidyā*, the particle of exclusion should precede the thesis (*pakṣa*) and follow the reason (*hetu*). Here, however, the reason is placed first and the thesis follows;

this constitutes an inversion, which is stated to be a fault. The five types of pseudo-dissimilar examples are concluded. This concludes the three preceding explanations of pseudo-examples. Below, the fourth section summarizes the previous headings.
Statements such as these, which resemble the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), are not genuine means of proof (*sādhana*).
This collectively concludes the preceding discussion on fallacious theses, reasons, and examples, totaling thirty-three faults;
therefore, they are said to be "not genuine means of proof. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the preceding section. This concludes the two preceding explanations on the gate of fallacious means of proof.
[End. The following three sections explain the gate of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, for the sake of one’s own awakening, it should be known that there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): direct perception and inference (*anumāna*).

Herein, direct perception is defined as being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). If there is correct cognition regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which is devoid of all conceptual constructions such as names and categories, it is "directly manifest" (*pratyakṣa*).
It is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it functions differently [from inference].

Furthermore, below, the two means of valid cognition are indicated together: since both direct perception and inference have as their object that which is personally realized and personally understood, it is said to be "for one’s own awakening.
Herein, direct perception refers to that which is non-conceptual; this definitively identifies direct perception.
"Direct perception" (*pramāṇa*) means the non-arising of conceptual construction. To explain this, [the text] says "if there is... and so forth.

This means that when correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) arises, one does not give rise to any conceptual construction based on the seeds of names and phrases regarding form, sound, odor, taste, or touch; yet, one is able to engage with each of the five objects as they manifest before one.
Therefore, it is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The "seeds of names and phrases" refers to those produced by habitual conditioning (*vāsanā*). This clarifies [the point].
The meaning of "becoming a seed" refers to the process of non-forgetting through mindfulness and the perfuming of mental impressions (*vāsanā*).

For example, when a child sees a form with the eyes, they think, "it is a form," and this is accumulated in the mind; when they hear a sound with the ears, they think, "it is a sound," and this is accumulated in the mind.
Through accumulation day after day and month after month, these are perfumed to form seeds, which later arise from those seeds within the gateway of sounds and forms.

Sounds, forms, names, and phrases are what are called "name-seeds" (*nāma-bīja*). What is now being explained is the state free from all such conceptual discrimination regarding name-seeds and the like.
Furthermore, the phrase "each appearing and turning distinctly" refers to the meaning of non-discrimination within the gates of sound and form.
Just as images appear in a mirror, vivid and distinct, so too do the five sense objects appear and turn distinctly; yet, like a mirror, there is no obstruction or lingering attachment.
It is free from all conceptual constructions based on names and categories. △ The third section, the explanation of the gate of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is concluded.

Below, the fourth section explains the gate of inference (*anumāna*). Regarding inference: it refers to observing an object by means of various signs (*liṅga*). There are three kinds of signs, as previously explained.

With that [inference] as its cause, there arises a correct cognition regarding the object of inference, such as the realization that "there is fire" or "it is impermanent," and this is called *anumāna* (inference).

Among the two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this cognition itself is termed the "result" (*phala*) because it is the characteristic of realization and because it manifests as having a functional operation;
it is also termed a "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding the term "inference" (*anumāna*): this is the heading that introduces the section. "That which observes an object by means of various marks" explains the two characters *anumāna*:
"various marks" explains *anu*, and "observing the object" explains *māna*. The phrase "marks exist... and so forth explains the establishment of "various marks.

Regarding the statement "there are three types," these are the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). "As has already been explained before" refers to what was previously stated in the section on the "means of proof" (*sādhana*).

[The opponent] asks: "What is the difference between these three characteristics [of the thesis] and those [three characteristics] within the reason (*hetu*)? [The respondent] answers: "The three characteristics within the reason belong exclusively to the reason;

they serve as the reason for the thesis (*pakṣa*) and are termed 'the means of establishment' (*sādhana*). The three characteristics here [in the syllogism] subsume all three members [of the syllogism];

they serve as the cause for cognition and are termed 'inference' (*anumāna*). Therefore, they are not the same. From the words "By that... below, he explains inference (*anumāna*), stating: "It is by means of non-existence..."

The three members [of the syllogism] serve as the cause, while the arising of inferential cognition (*anumāna-jñāna*) constitutes the result. Therefore, it is said that regarding the object of inference, there arises correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*).
Once this correct cognition has arisen, one clearly knows the presence of fire, impermanence, and so forth; this is the meaning of inference (*anumāna*).

Regarding the statement that among the two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), "cognition itself is called the result," this refers to both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference, as both take the arising of cognition as their result. As for inference:
Inference has the three members as its cause and produces non-conceptual correct cognition (*nirvikalpa-samyagjñāna*) as its fruit, because it is capable of realizing the object to be inferred.

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has form and so forth as its cause and produces non-conceptual correct cognition as its fruit, because it is capable of realizing the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so forth;
thus it is said to be "the characteristic of realization. Because it manifests with functional activity, it is also called [direct perception].
Regarding "as measures": this specifically clarifies the measures of the world, such as [the measure of] time and so forth. That is to say, the function of flux manifests the measure of time;
the function of atomic particles manifests the measure of number; the function of obstructive matter manifests the measure of form; and the function of insentient space...

The manifestation of the measure of emptiness is the function of curvature; the manifestation of the measure of form is the function of luminosity; the manifestation of the measure of shadow is likewise.
Since all such measures are manifested through their functions, this concludes the fourth section: the explanation of the gate of inference (*anumāna*). Below is the fifth section:
the explanation of the gate of fallacious direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

There is conceptual cognition that operates differently with respect to its object; this is called "pseudo-perception. That is to say, various cognitions that apprehend jars, garments, and so forth arise through conceptualization.
Because they do not take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objective domain with respect to the object, they are called pseudo-perception.

Cognition possesses conceptualization; within all phenomena, it does not realize their intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), but rather arises in accordance with verbal designations, which is termed "erroneous transformation.

Because it fails to comprehend meanings such as impermanence, and because it is not inference (*anumāna*), but merely a conceptualization based on the seeds of verbal designations arising in accordance with what is seen or heard, it is called "pseudo-perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). Therefore, the commentary states: "That is to say, for those who possess cognition..."

The [cognitions] of jars, clothing, and so forth arise from conceptual differentiation. Why is this? Because they do not take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object as their objective domain.
△ The fifth section, the explanation of the pseudo-perceptual gate, is concluded. Below, the sixth section explains the pseudo-inferential gate.
If a cognition based on a fallacious reason arises prior to it, then the various cognitions of objects that appear similar [to the real] are called "fallacious inference" (*tarka*).

There are many kinds of fallacious reasons, as previously explained; when these are employed as reasons, cognitions arise regarding what appears to be the object of inference, yet they are unable to provide correct understanding.
It is called "pseudo-inference" (*pramāṇābhāsa*).
Regarding "pseudo-reasoning cognition" (*hetvābhāsa-jñāna*): "reasoning" (*hetu*) refers to inference; thus, the cognition produced by pseudo-inference is termed "pseudo-reasoning cognition.
As for the phrase "the cognitions of pseudo-objects previously arisen are called pseudo-inference," this refers to the three aforementioned types [of pseudo-reasons] that carry faults.

[The term] "branch" (*aṅga*). Among various objects, although it appears as if there is something known, one cannot correctly comprehend meanings such as impermanence; this is merely termed "semblance-inference" (*tulya-anumāna*).
Below the section on the "many kinds of semblance-reasons," the [text] provides an explanation for its establishment, stating that thirty-three fallacies have already been discussed previously.

It is called "multiple" (aneka), which is to say "many. Because it takes those multiple faults as its reason (*hetu*), although a cognition arises regarding the object of inference (*anumeya-artha*), one cannot correctly understand it;
therefore, it is termed "pseudo" (*ābhāsa*). △ The sixth section, the explanation of the gate of pseudo-inference (*anumānābhāsa*), is concluded.
The following seven points explain the gate of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, that which reveals the faults of the proof (*sādhana*) is called refutation.

This refers to the initial proof’s deficiency, the fault of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetu-asiddha*), the inconclusive nature of the reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*), the contradictory nature of the reason (*viruddha-hetu*), and the faults of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The term "nature" (*svabhāva*) indicates this statement; because it clarifies and instructs the questioner, it is called "the refuter" (*dūṣaṇa*).
Within the section on "establishment" (*sādhana*), that which can correctly reveal any fault is the meaning of "refutation. This refers to the first [category].

This explains the establishment [of the thesis] and reveals its faults. First, regarding the "prover" (*sādhana*): this refers to the subject (*pakṣa*) as previously stated. It is based upon that *dharmin* (the substratum) that the thesis can be established.
If it is fully accomplished, it is called the "complete establishment of the *dharmin*"; if there is even a slight deficiency, it is not so.
To speak of these as faults: the faults of the thesis (*pakṣa*) are the nine types mentioned previously; the unestablished reasons (*asiddha-hetu*) are the four types mentioned previously;
the inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika-hetu*) are the six types mentioned previously; the contradictory reasons (*viruddha-hetu*) are the four types mentioned previously;
and the faulty examples (*dṛṣṭānta-doṣa*) are the ten types mentioned previously. If one can clearly demonstrate these thirty-three kinds of faulty statements, one will enlighten the questioner.

Thus, it is called "capable refutation. △ The seventh section, the explanation of the gate of capable refutation, is concluded. Below is the eighth section, the explanation of the gate of pseudo-capable refutation.
If one does not truly manifest a fault in the proof (sādhana), it is called "pseudo-capable refutation.

That is to say: to point out a deficiency in a complete proof; to speak of a faulty thesis when the thesis is faultless; or to speak of an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*) when the reason is established.

To speak of an "uncertain cause" when it is a "determinative cause," to speak of a "contradictory cause" when it is a "non-contradictory cause," and to speak of a "faulty example" when it is a "faultless example"—
such speech is called a "pseudo-refutation. Because it cannot reveal the faults of another's position,
as that [position] is actually faultless, let us now leave this matter aside.

Regarding the category of "pseudo-refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*), it may admit of two senses. First, if the proponent’s own position (*sthāpanā*) inherently contains a fault, yet the opponent is unable to correctly demonstrate that error, this constitutes a pseudo-refutation; for it fails to expose the flaw in the other's thesis.

Second, even if the proponent’s position is fundamentally without fault, to falsely accuse the opponent of error likewise does not constitute a genuine refutation, since the opponent is without fault. Furthermore...
Let this matter rest. The remaining meanings are as stated in the text; the wording shall not be prolix. △ The eighth section, the explanation of the "pseudo-refutation" gate, is concluded.

Having briefly proclaimed a few words of meaning, I have established one corner as a starting point; the subtle discernment between what is rational and irrational therein shall be found in other places.
That is to say, having already expounded a few subtle words of meaning, I have established one corner as a beginning and expanded upon it; thus, the six directions [of the universe] are encompassed.

All are thus. If one attains their essential meaning, then within the gateway of sound and form, one not only understands the significance of the permanent and the impermanent, but there are also those who directly realize the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Among these, what constitutes "reason" (*yukti*) refers to the aforementioned three types of faultless [inference];
what constitutes "unreason" (*ayukti*) refers to the aforementioned thirty-three fallacies. These have been elegantly analyzed elsewhere; they are all contained herein as reason and unreason.
